summary: Provides basic terminology for constrained-node networks, in which small devices have severe limits on power, memory, and processing. The terms, such as device classes by capability, have been useful in standardization work on the Internet of Things.

eli5.summary: Tiny gadgets like sensors have very little brainpower and battery. This document gives everyone the same words to talk about how small and weak these gadgets are.

questions: what are class 0 1 and 2 constrained devices
what is the difference between constrained and challenged networks
subtitle: Shared vocabulary for tiny, power-limited devices and the networks they form: node classes, energy classes and power strategies.

tldr.problem: The Internet Protocol Suite is increasingly used on small devices with severe limits on power, memory and processing, and different groups needed consistent words for them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines constrained node, constrained network and constrained-node network, sorts devices into Class 0, 1 and 2 by data and code size, and adds codes for energy limitation (E0, E1, E2, E9) and power strategy (P0, P1, P9).
tldr.outcome: It is a terminology reference, not a protocol, and the classes are rough indications that the RFC expects to shift over time.

today: RFC 7228 is an Informational document with no listed obsoleting or updating RFC. It defines vocabulary only, and its own text expects the class boundaries to move over time.

sections.title: Why Terms for Constrained Devices
sections.content:
Small devices with limited CPU, memory and power, often used as sensors or actuators, can form a network and become constrained nodes. The network itself may also be constrained, with lossy channels, limited and unpredictable bandwidth and a highly dynamic topology.

The RFC says its aim is not to cover the field exhaustively but to make sure a few core terms are used consistently between groups working in this space. It also fixes some usage: a "byte" is an octet, "KiB" is 1024 bytes, and "power" means electrical power, not processing power.
sections.eli5: Many tiny gadgets are being connected, and people need the same words for how small and weak they are.

sections.title: Core Terminology
sections.content:
A constrained node is one where characteristics normally taken for granted on Internet nodes are not attainable, often because of cost, size, weight or available power. Tight limits on power, memory and processing set hard bounds on state, code space and processing cycles, so saving energy and bandwidth dominates the design. The RFC admits this is not a rigorous definition.

A constrained network is one where link-layer characteristics taken for granted are not attainable, for example low throughput, high or highly variable packet loss, asymmetric links, penalties for larger packets, and no IP multicast. A constrained-node network is one influenced by having a significant portion of constrained nodes, and it is always also a constrained network.

A challenged network is a further step: it has serious trouble keeping the end-to-end IP model, for example with interruptions or delay well beyond the TCP Maximum Segment Lifetime. All challenged networks are constrained, but not the reverse. The RFC also mentions two related terms it does not define: LLN (Low-Power and Lossy Network, from RFC 7102) and LoWPAN or 6LoWPAN.
sections.eli5: A weak gadget, a bad road and a town full of weak gadgets each get their own name, so people know which problem they are talking about.

sections.title: Classes of Constrained Devices
sections.content:
Table 1 gives rough classes by data size (such as RAM) and code size (such as Flash). They match clusters of commercially available chips at the time of writing, and the RFC expects the boundaries to move.

  • Class 0: very constrained sensor-like motes. They most likely cannot talk to the Internet securely on their own and use larger devices as proxies, gateways or servers.
  • Class 1: too limited for a full stack with HTTP, TLS and XML, but able to use a stack made for constrained nodes such as CoAP over UDP, and to act as peers without a gateway.
  • Class 2: fundamentally able to support most of the protocol stacks used on notebooks or servers, though lightweight protocols can still help them.

The RFC defines no classes beyond Class 2, since such devices can largely use existing protocols unchanged.
sections.eli5: Class 0 is a tiny helper that needs a grown-up to speak for it, Class 1 can talk for itself in simple words, and Class 2 can nearly talk like a grown-up.

sections.title: Power Terminology
sections.content:
Available power can range from kilowatts to microwatts. Rather than classes, the RFC suggests quoting two quantities in SI units: Ps, the sustainable average power in watts, and Et, the total energy available before the source is exhausted, in joules.

Energy limitation is classified as E0 (limited for a single event, such as an energy-harvesting light switch), E1 (limited per period, such as a battery recharged or replaced periodically), E2 (limited over the whole lifetime, such as a non-replaceable primary battery) and E9 (no direct limit, such as mains power).

Strategies for using power to communicate are P0 normally-off (reattach when needed), P1 low-power (appears connected, perhaps with high latency) and P9 always-on. RFC 7102 distinguishes only Non-Sleepy Nodes (P9) and Sleepy Nodes (P0).
sections.eli5: Some gadgets get a battery for one press, some for a day, some for life, and some plug into the wall. They also differ in how often they wake up to chat.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document introduces only terminology and says it raises no new security issues. Security issues arising from the constraints must be discussed for each specific protocol. As pointers, it names the constrained node considerations section of the CoAP specification, a threat analysis for RPL, and work on implementing security protocols on constrained nodes.
sections.eli5: Words alone do not make anything unsafe, but each real gadget protocol has to think about its own safety.

items.label: Class 0
items.desc: Data size much less than 10 KiB, code size much less than 100 KiB.

items.label: Class 1
items.desc: Data size about 10 KiB, code size about 100 KiB.

items.label: Class 2
items.desc: Data size about 50 KiB, code size about 250 KiB.

items.label: Period energy-limited
items.desc: Example: battery that is periodically recharged or replaced.
